hook.text: The newest pipelines don't end in a dashboard. They feed an AI assistant, which can only answer from what's in its index.

hook-steps.text: Extract, clean, split, embed, index, keep fresh, delete. The fundamentals carry over. What's new is the vector store, and the embedding bill.

plan.text: Eleven questions, and every one gets worked through.

changed.text: Question one. How have Data Engineer interviews changed with AI? The core hasn't: sequel, modeling, and batch and streaming design.

changed-layer.text: On top: system design for AI data. Unstructured data, PDFs and tickets parsed into clean text. Vector search trade-offs. And AI in your own workflow.

changed-verify.text: Some coding rounds allow an assistant, and grade how you check its code: idempotency, partition overwrites, time zones, schema drift.

rag.text: Question two. Walk through the ingestion pipeline for a RAG assistant. RAG is retrieval-augmented generation: find the passages, then answer from them.

rag-halves.text: Two halves. Offline, a pipeline builds the index. Online, each question is embedded, searched with a filter, reranked, and the best hits fill the prompt.

rag-extract.text: Most of the work is offline. Extract incrementally, with change data capture or an updated-at watermark. Parse and clean: strip boilerplate, keep headings and tables, drop duplicates.

rag-meta.text: Chunk, then attach metadata to each chunk: document id, section, timestamps, and who may read it. That makes filters, citations and deletes possible.

rag-upsert.text: Last, embed and upsert, keyed by a stable chunk id, so a retried batch overwrites instead of duplicating.

chunk.text: Question three. How do you choose a chunking strategy? It's precision against context. Small chunks match precisely, but can lose the context the answer needs.

chunk-large.text: Large chunks keep context, but one vector must cover several topics, so retrieval gets fuzzier, and each hit takes more of the context window.

chunk-fixed.text: Common choices: a fixed size, say three to five hundred tokens, overlapping ten to twenty percent, so a sentence cut at a boundary is whole in one chunk.

chunk-struct.text: Structure-aware: split on headings and paragraphs, then merge toward the target. Or small-to-big: retrieve small chunks, send the parent section.

chunk-measure.text: No universal best: measure retrieval recall on labeled real questions, and store the chunk settings with the index version, since changing them means a rebuild.

fresh.text: Question four. How do you keep embeddings fresh without re-embedding everything? Treat it as an incremental load: give every chunk a stable id and a content hash, and compare with what's indexed.

fresh-run.text: In the page's example, doc one, chunk one changed, and doc three is new: embed those two. Doc two is gone: delete it. Doc one, chunk zero costs nothing.

fresh-leak.text: Skip the deletes, and a removed document keeps answering questions. Wrong at best, a data leak at worst.

switch.text: Question five. What changes when you switch embedding models? Everything gets re-embedded. Each model has its own space, so a new model's query can't be compared with old documents.

switch-demo.text: Here's a tiny space of five words. Pretend a second model learned the same meanings with its axes in another order. Its kitten, searched in the old index, lands nearest truck.

switch-bg.text: So treat it like a blue-green deployment: build a new index version beside the old, backfill and compare, then switch an alias atomically, and keep the old one for rollback.

switch-tag.text: And store the model version on every vector, so a mixed index can't happen silently.

ann.text: Question six. Exact or approximate nearest-neighbor search? Exact search compares the query with every vector: perfectly accurate, and fine into the hundreds of thousands, especially after a filter.

ann-index.text: Beyond that, approximate indexes trade a little recall for big speedups. HNSW, a graph index, is fast and accurate, but memory-hungry and slow to build. A cluster index searches only the clusters nearest the query.

ann-sim.text: Model it in NumPy: twenty thousand vectors in a hundred clusters. Probe one cluster, and you compare one percent of the vectors and find about seventy percent of the true top ten. Probe sixteen: ninety-six.

ann-measure.text: That's the knob. Measure recall against exact search on a sample; don't trust the defaults.

pg.text: Question seven. Should you use pgvector or a dedicated vector database? pgvector, the Postgres extension, is a strong default if the data's in Postgres and it's millions of vectors, not billions.

pg-why.text: One system, real transactions, joins against your relational data, and access filters in plain sequel.

pg-dedicated.text: A dedicated vector database earns its operational cost at very large scale, very high query rates, or when you need hybrid search and multi-tenancy built in.

pg-lean.text: Say which way you'd lean, and what evidence would change your mind.

filter.text: Question eight. Why do metadata filters make vector search harder? Because the index is built for similarity, not for your filter.

filter-post.text: Post-filtering searches first, then drops what the user may not see. A selective filter leaves far fewer results than you asked for.

filter-sim.text: In the same simulation, give each vector one of a hundred tenants. Take the top ten, keep one tenant's, and ninety-one percent of searches come back empty.

filter-pre.text: Pre-filtering restricts first, then searches. That's correct, but it can defeat the approximate index, which was built over everything.

filter-fix.text: Good answers partition by tenant, use an engine that filters during the search, and test with realistic, selective filters.

hybrid.text: Question nine. What is hybrid search, and when do embeddings alone fail? Embeddings capture meaning, but blur exact tokens: error codes, product codes, names, rare jargon.

hybrid-code.text: Search the tickets for E four oh three one, and the vector side ranks the ticket with that code fourth, behind general errors.

hybrid-bm25.text: Hybrid search adds a keyword search, usually BM25. Like TF-IDF, it weighs words by rarity, so a code in one ticket counts for a lot.

hybrid-rrf.text: Then fuse the rankings with reciprocal rank fusion: each list gives a ticket one over sixty plus its rank, summed. Fourth by meaning and first by keyword, the code's ticket wins.

hybrid-cheap.text: It's cheap to add, and it usually helps on technical content.

access.text: Question ten. How do access control and deletion work in a RAG pipeline? Put permissions on each chunk, and filter at query time by the user's identity, so the assistant retrieves only what that user could open.

access-redact.text: Redact secrets and personal data before embedding, above all if the embedding model is an outside API.

access-delete.text: And make deletion real. An erasure request or a removed document deletes the vectors, the cached chunks and any copies in evaluation sets, not just the source row.

backfill.text: Question eleven, the last. How do you estimate the cost and time of an embedding backfill? Count tokens: ten million chunks at about four hundred tokens is four billion.

backfill-div.text: For cost, that's four thousand times the price per million tokens. For time, divide by your rate limit: at a million tokens a minute, four thousand minutes, nearly three days.

backfill-fail.text: So design for failure partway: batch the requests, retry with backoff on rate limits, checkpoint progress, and upsert idempotently, so a restart resumes rather than starting over.

backfill-hash.text: And content hashing pays for itself again: an unchanged chunk is never embedded twice.

close.text: Eleven questions, and the same habits under all of them: load incrementally, write idempotently, and make a delete really delete.

close-practice.text: That closes the series. Every topic page has concept checks, and a bank of a hundred and ten multiple-choice questions shows which rounds need work.
